en.heading: Why Spartan exists
points: Spartan exists to help people push beyond their limits
The aim: people who are stronger, physically and mentally
The mission: to help people live without limits
en.narration: Spartan exists to help people push beyond their limits and become stronger, physically and mentally. Its mission is to help people live without limits, by building the strength, discipline and resilience they need to face life's challenges. Every Spartan Race is designed to make athletes do something hard, uncomfortable and transformative. That is the setting you work in as a referee. The athletes in front of you have chosen to do something difficult, and the rules exist so that they all face the same test.

en.heading: A challenge for everyone
points: Spartan events are for all levels, from first-time racers to elite competitors
Millions of people around the world take part
What matters is the willingness to show up, not where you start
en.narration: Spartan events are designed for athletes of every level. Millions of people around the world take part, from first-time racers to elite competitors. Spartan's view is that what matters is not where you start, but the willingness to show up, push past excuses and confront the challenge. Everyone who steps onto the course takes part in the same test of grit and determination. So on race day you will see a wide range of athletes. Later in this course you will learn which of them you officiate most closely.

en.heading: One set of rules, everywhere
points: The Rules of Competition apply to all Spartan events and competitions globally
They are binding on every competitor at every Spartan event
Their aims: fair and consistent racing, global standards, competitor safety
en.narration: The Spartan Rules of Competition apply to all Spartan events and competitions around the world, and they are binding on every competitor taking part. The rulebook says the rules explain how a race should be officiated. They aim to make every event fair and consistent, run with sportsmanship and integrity. They give clear guidelines, so that competition is standardised globally. And they protect the health, safety and well-being of competitors, as far as that can reasonably be achieved in obstacle course racing.

en.heading: Your part in it
points: Apply the competition rules and officiating procedures consistently
Protect the fairness and integrity of Spartan events worldwide
By the end of this course: apply the rules consistently and confidently
en.narration: This programme introduces the role, responsibilities and standards expected of Spartan referees. Its goal is that every referee applies the competition rules and the officiating procedures in the same way, protecting the fairness and integrity of Spartan events worldwide. An athlete should get the same decision at your obstacle as they would at the same obstacle at any other Spartan event. By the end of the course, you should be able to apply Spartan rules consistently and confidently.

en.heading: In short
points: Spartan exists to help people push beyond their limits
Its events are for everyone, from first-timers to elite competitors
One rulebook applies to every Spartan event worldwide
Your job: apply it consistently, to protect fairness and integrity
en.narration: In short. Spartan exists to help people push beyond their limits and become stronger in body and mind. Its events are for everyone, from first-time racers to elite competitors. One set of rules applies to every Spartan event in the world, and it aims for racing that is fair, consistent and safe. Your job as a referee is to apply those rules consistently, so that the fairness and integrity of every race is protected.

en.heading: Trail running with obstacles
points: A Spartan Race is an obstacle course race (OCR)
It combines trail running with physical obstacles
The obstacles test both mental and physical strength
en.narration: A Spartan Race is an obstacle course race: trail running combined with physical obstacles along the course. The obstacles are designed to test both mental and physical strength, and to push racers beyond what they thought possible. Between the obstacles, athletes run. At each obstacle, they have to overcome a particular challenge, and the rulebook sets out exactly what that involves. As a referee you are usually posted at an obstacle, so that obstacle and its rules are your focus for the day.

en.heading: Five kinds of challenge
points: Climbing: for example the walls and the Rope Climb
Carrying: for example the Bucket Carry and the Sandbag Carry
Crawling: for example the Barbed Wire Crawl
Jumping, and pulling and lifting: for example the Fire Jump and the Hercules Hoist
en.narration: The programme groups the challenges into five kinds of movement: climbing, carrying, crawling, jumping, and pulling and lifting. Climbing includes the walls and the Rope Climb. Carrying includes the Bucket Carry and the Sandbag Carry. Crawling includes the Barbed Wire Crawl. Jumping includes the Fire Jump, and pulling and lifting includes the Hercules Hoist, where the athlete pulls a rope to raise a weight. Each obstacle has its own section in the rulebook, setting out what the athlete must do and how they can fail.

en.heading: Two kinds of obstacle in the rulebook
points: Mandatory obstacles: must be completed before going further on the course
Pass/fail obstacles: a fail means a penalty, a penalty loop or burpees
Every obstacle must be attempted: at a minimum, touched
en.narration: The rulebook separates obstacles into two categories. Mandatory obstacles must be completed before the athlete goes any further on the course. Failing one means disqualification, although the Race Director can substitute a time penalty, depending on how serious it is. Pass or fail obstacles can be failed, and a fail means a penalty: a penalty loop or burpees. Pass or fail obstacles are either single attempt or multiple attempt. Every obstacle must be attempted, and an attempt is, at a minimum, touching it. Obstacle types have their own section later in this course.
en.review: Under review for 2027: the rulebook (3.17.3) says the penalty is a penalty loop or 30 burpees, as Spartan designates for each event, category or heat. The Officiating SOP says a loop for most obstacles and burpees at the Spear Throw; the 2026 programme says burpees are used only at the Spear Throw. Meanwhile, use the penalty confirmed at your briefing and refer any doubt to the Head Referee.

en.heading: Race formats
points: The 2026 sources name the Sprint, Super, Beast, Ultra and Stadion formats
One rulebook covers them all, but some rules differ by format
Stadion: the penalty for failing any obstacle is always 15 burpees
Minimum referees: 10 at a Sprint or Stadion, 15 at a Super, 20 at a Beast or Ultra
en.narration: Spartan races come in several formats. The 2026 rulebook and officiating procedure name the Sprint, Super, Beast, Ultra and Stadion. The same rulebook covers them all, but some rules differ by format. At Stadion events, for example, the penalty for failing an obstacle is always fifteen burpees, for every obstacle and every heat. Spartan's officiating procedure also sets a minimum number of referees for each format: ten for a Sprint or a Stadion, fifteen for a Super, and twenty for a Beast or an Ultra.

en.heading: In short
points: An obstacle course race: trail running combined with physical obstacles
Five kinds of challenge: climbing, carrying, crawling, jumping, pulling and lifting
Mandatory obstacles must be completed; failing a pass/fail obstacle means a penalty
Formats: Sprint, Super, Beast, Ultra and Stadion
en.narration: In short. A Spartan Race is an obstacle course race: trail running combined with physical obstacles that test mental and physical strength. The challenges are climbing, carrying, crawling, jumping, and pulling and lifting. The rulebook splits obstacles into mandatory obstacles, which must be completed, and pass or fail obstacles, where a fail means a penalty. Every obstacle must be attempted. Races come in several formats, including the Sprint, Super, Beast, Ultra and Stadion.

en.heading: What referees protect
points: Fairness and the integrity of the race
Athletes following the official rules of competition
Penalties applied consistently
Credibility for Elite and competitive racing
en.narration: Referees matter because they protect the fairness and integrity of the race. They make sure athletes follow the official rules of competition, and they apply penalties in the same way for everyone. That consistency is what gives Elite and competitive racing its credibility. Spartan's officiating procedure puts it this way: Spartan officiating establishes and maintains race integrity through consistent enforcement of the rules and standard officiating practice, so that the outcome is fair and equitable for all athletes.

en.heading: What a referee is
points: A Spartan-appointed official who makes sure all the rules are followed
Usually posted at an obstacle, or in the video review tent
At your obstacle: enforce its rules and monitor failures
You report to the Head Referee
en.narration: The rulebook defines a referee as a Spartan-appointed official whose task is to make sure all the rules are followed. Referees are usually posted at obstacles and in the video review tent, and they report to the Head Official. Spartan's officiating procedure describes the referee as the person assigned to an obstacle to enforce its rules and monitor failures. In the rulebook, officials are anyone Spartan designates to carry out event duties in a position of authority: staff, referees and volunteers. As a referee, you are one of them.

en.heading: Who you answer to
points: The Head Referee: the chief decision maker on the rules at the event
The rulebook calls this role the Head Official
The Race Director: responsible for the overall operation of the event
Uncertain or disputed calls go to the Head Referee
en.narration: At every event, one person is the chief decision maker on all matters of the rules, and the ultimate authority for enforcing and interpreting them. The rulebook calls this person the Head Official. Spartan's officiating procedure and this programme call them the Head Referee. That is who you report to. The Race Director is responsible for the overall operations and running of the event. When you are unsure about a call, or an athlete disputes one, it goes to the Head Referee.

en.heading: Your calls reach the results
points: The chain: referee, Head Referee, then Race Director or timing team
The Head Referee confirms penalties and passes them on
Results are final only after the official video review
Time penalties are added to the athlete's finish time
en.narration: What you see and record at your obstacle can change the results. The chain runs from you, to the Head Referee, to the Race Director or the timing team. The Head Referee manages video review, and passes confirmed penalties and disqualifications on to the Race Director and the timing team. The rulebook says an official video review should take place before results are final, so results may not be posted straight away. Time penalties are added to the athlete's finish time, so an accurate, clearly recorded call matters.

en.heading: How you are trained
points: Based on the Spartan Rulebook, the Officiating SOP and the Global Officiating Guidelines
Focus: obstacle enforcement, penalties, athlete interaction and race integrity
Completing the online training is mandatory for referee certification
en.narration: This training exists so that referees enforce Spartan's competition rules fairly and consistently. It is based on three documents: the Spartan Rulebook, the Officiating Standard Operating Procedure, and the Global Officiating Guidelines. It focuses on obstacle enforcement, penalties, how you deal with athletes, and the integrity of the competition. Under the officiating procedure, completing the online training module is mandatory for referee certification. Before each event, the Head Referee also makes sure that every referee has completed pre-event training.

en.heading: In short
points: Referees protect fairness, race integrity and consistent penalties
You enforce the rules at your obstacle and monitor failures
You report to the Head Referee, the final authority on the rules
Your calls feed the video review and the results
en.narration: In short. Referees protect the fairness and integrity of the race, and make sure penalties are applied consistently, which gives competitive racing its credibility. You are a Spartan-appointed official, usually posted at an obstacle, there to enforce its rules and monitor failures. You report to the Head Referee, whom the rulebook calls the Head Official, and who has the final say on the rules. What you record goes through video review and can change an athlete's finish time.

en.heading: Competitive and Open
points: Competitive: Elite and Age Group racers
Open: open to everyone, the participation-focused category
Each category starts in heats or waves, separated by start time or pace group
en.narration: The rulebook defines two kinds of category. Competitive, which includes Elite and Age Group, and Open, which is open to everyone. This programme describes Open as the participation-focused category. Within each category, athletes start in heats and waves: groups separated by their start times or by pace group. Knowing which category is coming through your obstacle tells you how closely you need to officiate it.

en.heading: Where referees focus
points: Referees focus primarily on the Competitive categories
Competitive racers are expected to follow every rule explicitly
Enforce the rules the same way for every Competitive racer
Be in position before the first Elite start
en.narration: Referees focus primarily on the Competitive categories: Elite and Age Group. The rulebook expects every Competitive racer to follow all the rules explicitly, and to race in a spirited and competitive manner. So your enforcement must be the same for every Competitive racer, in every Elite and Age Group wave. Spartan's officiating procedure says the Head Referee confirms that referees are in position before the first Elite start, and that officiating, video review and penalty assessment are for the Elite and Age Group categories.

en.heading: Open racers
points: Open racers are encouraged to follow the rules too
The atmosphere is more relaxed: sportsmanship and personal accountability
Open racers are expected to use Spartan honour for burpee penalties
Referees may clear down, or hand over to volunteers, for the Open waves
en.narration: Open racers are also encouraged to follow the rules, in the spirit of sportsmanship and personal accountability, even though the atmosphere in the Open category is more relaxed. The rulebook expects Open category competitors to use Spartan honour when they complete burpee penalties. In this programme, the referee's event timeline ends with clearing down the course, or handing over to volunteers for the Open waves. Your Head Referee's briefing will tell you which applies at your event.

en.heading: Heats, waves and timing
points: Racers must start in their assigned heat, wave or group
An Elite racer who starts in the wrong heat is moved to Open
Elite heats: the first across the finish line wins (gun time)
Age Group, Open and Elite Stadion heats: chip time. Both add any time penalties
en.narration: Every racer must start in and with their assigned heat, wave or group. A racer who starts in the wrong heat is not eligible for awards, and an Elite racer who starts in the wrong heat is moved to the Open category. Timing differs by category. In an Elite heat, the winner is whoever crosses the finish line first, which is called gun time. Age Group and Open heats, and Elite heats at Stadion, use chip time: from crossing the start line to crossing the finish. Either way, any time penalties are added.

en.heading: In short
points: Competitive means Elite and Age Group; Open is open to everyone
Referees focus primarily on Competitive racers
Every Competitive racer gets the same enforcement
Open racers are encouraged to follow the rules, on Spartan honour
en.narration: In short. There are two kinds of category: Competitive, which is Elite and Age Group, and Open, which is open to everyone. Referees focus primarily on the Competitive categories, where racers are expected to follow every rule, and your enforcement must be the same for every one of them. Open racers are encouraged to follow the rules too, in a more relaxed atmosphere and on Spartan honour. Elite heats are won on gun time, the others on chip time, with any time penalties added.

en.heading: Impartial and professional
points: Be impartial: apply the rules the same way to every athlete
Be professional: calm, neutral and respectful
Know the Competition Rules and the Officiating SOP
en.narration: The referee mindset starts with being impartial and professional. Spartan's officiating procedure asks you to apply the obstacle rules consistently and impartially, whoever the athlete is. Stay calm, neutral and respectful, and represent Spartan professionally. Your two key documents are the Spartan Competition Rules and the Officiating Standard Operating Procedure. Familiarise yourself with both before the event, and make sure you know and understand the rules for your own obstacle.

en.heading: Rule intent, fairness and safety
points: Focus on the intent of the rule, not on minor accidental contact
Ask whether the athlete gained an advantage
Put fairness and athlete safety first
en.narration: Focus on what a rule is there for, not on minor accidental contact. One of the programme's scenarios is an athlete who briefly touches the top of an obstacle but gains no advantage. The question to consider is whether an advantage was created. Put fairness and athlete safety first. Protecting the health, safety and well-being of competitors is one of the rulebook's stated aims. If you see a safety concern at your obstacle, report it straight away to the Head Referee or the Race Director.

en.heading: When unsure, escalate
points: Escalate any situation you are unsure about
Unsure of the penalty or how to enforce it: contact the Head Referee at once
Doubts, safety concerns or inconsistencies: report them straight away
en.narration: You are not expected to settle every situation on your own. When you are unsure, escalate. Spartan's officiating procedure says that if there is any uncertainty about the penalty type or how to enforce it, you contact the Head Referee immediately. When you arrive at your obstacle, report any doubts, safety concerns or inconsistencies straight away to the Race Director or the Head Referee. The Head Referee is the final authority on the rules at the event, so escalating is part of doing the job well.

en.heading: Before race day
points: Complete the pre-event training before you take part
It covers the rulebook, with emphasis on high-failure obstacles
It also covers the referee workflow, burpee standards and video at the Spear Throw
You receive a briefing package and access to video tutorials
en.narration: Your timeline starts before race day. The Head Referee makes sure every referee completes standard pre-event training before taking part. It covers the Spartan Rulebook, with emphasis on high-failure obstacles, which are the ones athletes fail most often. It also covers the referee process and workflow, burpee standards and how to enforce them, and video recording and review, which is used at the Spear Throw only. You also receive a pre-event briefing package and access to the official video tutorials.

en.heading: Race morning
points: Check in, confirm your obstacle and collect your equipment
Attend the Head Referee's mandatory onsite briefing
Reach your obstacle in good time before the first competitive wave
Inspect the obstacle, walk the penalty loop and choose where to stand
en.narration: On race morning, report to the tent you have been told to use, sign in, confirm your obstacle assignment and collect your equipment. Join the communication channel if one is used. Attend the Head Referee's mandatory onsite briefing. Then travel to your obstacle with enough time before the first competitive wave. There, inspect the setup, check which way athletes approach, walk the whole penalty loop, and decide where to stand so you can clearly see attempts, completions and failures.

en.heading: During the race and after
points: Officiate the Elite and competitive waves
Then clear down the course, or hand over to volunteers for the Open waves
On your return: footage goes to video review, written decisions to the Head Referee
Athletes take any protest to the Head Referee, within the protest period
en.narration: During the race, you officiate the Elite and competitive waves at your obstacle. After that, depending on the event, you clear down the course or hand over to volunteers for the Open waves. As referees return, the Head Referee manages video review of the footage. Where there is no video, your decisions are made on site, written down, and handed to the Head Referee when you get back. Results are final only after the official review. An athlete who wants to protest a penalty takes it to the Head Referee during the protest period.
en.review: Under review for 2027: the rulebook (3.19.1) says the protest period ends 15 minutes before the category's award ceremony. The Officiating SOP (4.2) gives half an hour before the ceremony as its example cut-off. Meanwhile, apply the rulebook, follow the protest times the Head Referee announces, and send any athlete with a protest to the Head Referee.

en.heading: In short
points: Be impartial, professional and consistent
Think about the rule's intent; put fairness and safety first
When unsure, escalate to the Head Referee
Your day: training, check-in, briefing, setup, officiating, handover
en.narration: In short. Be impartial and professional, and apply the rules the same way to every athlete. Focus on the intent of the rule rather than minor accidental contact, and put fairness and athlete safety first. When you are unsure, escalate to the Head Referee. Your event timeline runs from pre-event training and briefing, through check-in and equipment, obstacle inspection and setup, to officiating the competitive waves, and finally clearing down or handing over to volunteers for the Open waves.

en.heading: Reporting for duty
points: Report to the Volunteer Tent, or the referee tent, at your assigned reporting time
Sign in with the Volunteer Coordinator or the Head Referee
Confirm your obstacle assignment
Make yourself known to the Head Referee
en.narration: Your race day starts at check-in. Go to the Volunteer Tent, or the referee tent if your event uses one, at the reporting time you were given. Sign in with the Volunteer Coordinator or the Head Referee, and confirm which obstacle you have been assigned. Even if someone else signs you in, make sure the Head Referee knows you are there. Before the first Elite start, the Head Referee has to confirm that every referee is in position.

en.heading: What you collect at check-in
points: Official materials: referee tee, cap, credentials or other assigned equipment
The QR code sign for your obstacle, unless it is already in place
A place in the official communication channel, such as a WhatsApp group
en.narration: At check-in you receive your official officiating materials. That means your referee tee, cap and credentials, and any other equipment you have been assigned. Collect the QR code sign for your obstacle too, unless it is already positioned on site. It links to the video tutorial for that obstacle. Finally, make sure you are added to the official communication channel. That might be a WhatsApp group, another messaging platform, or a direct contact for the Head Referee.

en.heading: Your referee kit
points: Referee shirt or vest
A writing board or notebook, ideally waterproof
Printed rule sheets for your obstacle
A video camera and tripod, only when you are assigned one
en.narration: The 2026 programme lists what a referee needs at the obstacle. Wear your referee shirt or vest. Carry a writing board or notebook, ideally waterproof, because you will be recording headband numbers and notes, sometimes in wet conditions. Bring printed rule sheets for your obstacle, so you can check a rule on the spot. If you are assigned a camera, you will also have a video camera and a tripod.

en.heading: Bring your own essentials
points: A mobile phone
Clothing suited to the conditions
Pens or pencils, food and water
Anything personal you need, such as medication
en.narration: Bring your own essentials too. You need a mobile phone, because that is how you stay connected to the Head Referee through the communication channel. Wear clothing that suits the conditions on the day. Pack pens or pencils, food and water, and anything personal you need, such as medication. Once the competitive waves start, your attention belongs on your obstacle, so come prepared.

en.heading: The video kit
points: The Head Referee prepares, tests and hands out the officiating equipment
Cameras with at least 2.5 hours of battery, and backup batteries where needed
Adjustable 7 foot tripods, and SD cards of at least 32 GB for full HD
Video at the obstacles is for the Spear Throw only
en.narration: The officiating equipment is the Head Referee's responsibility. They prepare and test it on the Friday before the event, and hand it out on race day with final instructions. The procedure sets a minimum for the kit: video cameras with at least two and a half hours of battery, backup batteries, adjustable seven foot tripods, and memory cards of at least thirty two gigabytes, fast enough for full high definition. Video recording at obstacles is for the Spear Throw only. If you are given a camera there, you set it up and check it records before the first Elite wave.

en.heading: In short
points: Report to the tent on time, sign in and confirm your obstacle
Collect your materials and QR sign, and join the communication channel
Bring a waterproof board, rule sheets, phone, food and water
Camera and tripod only if you are assigned to film the Spear Throw
en.narration: In short. Report to the tent at your reporting time, sign in, confirm your obstacle and let the Head Referee know you are there. Collect your materials and the QR code sign for your obstacle, and join the communication channel. Bring a waterproof board or notebook, your rule sheets, your phone, food and water. You only carry a camera and tripod if you are assigned to film the Spear Throw.

en.heading: The briefing comes first
points: The Head Referee's onsite briefing is mandatory, before you deploy
It covers assignments, obstacle classifications, penalty loops and the burpee standard
It also covers event procedures and how penalties are reported
Then reach your obstacle in good time before the first competitive wave
en.narration: Before you go out on course, you attend the Head Referee's onsite briefing. It is mandatory. It covers the event's own procedures, where each obstacle is and who is assigned to it, which obstacles are mandatory and which allow multiple attempts, the penalty loops, the burpee standard, camera positioning at the Spear Throw, and how penalties are identified, reported and communicated. After the briefing, travel to your obstacle with enough time to prepare before the first competitive wave arrives.

en.heading: Know your obstacle's rules
points: Read your obstacle's instructions, failure modes and additional notes
Use the rule sheet, mission sheet and QR code video for your obstacle
Check for male and female options: on walls, the red step is for female athletes only
en.narration: Review and understand the rules for your obstacle before the first athlete arrives. In the rulebook, every obstacle has competitor instructions, failure modes and additional notes. Read all three. Your rule sheet, the obstacle mission sheet and the QR code video tutorial help too. Look out for different male and female options. On the six to nine foot walls, for example, the red step may be used by female athletes only, and a male athlete who uses it fails the obstacle.

en.heading: Inspect the setup
points: Inspect the obstacle setup and check it is serviceable
Review the race flow and the direction athletes approach from
Report doubts, safety concerns or inconsistencies at once to the Race Director or Head Referee
en.narration: When you arrive, inspect the obstacle. Check it is set up correctly and in a serviceable condition. Look at how the race flows through it and which direction athletes will approach from, so you know where they will arrive and where they will leave. If anything worries you, whether it is a doubt about the setup, a safety concern or something inconsistent, report it immediately to the Race Director or the Head Referee. Don't wait until the athletes arrive.

en.heading: Walk the penalty loop
points: Walk the whole penalty loop, where there is one
Know the route and exactly where athletes return to the course
Loops vary: running, carry, crawl or distance-based, as confirmed for your obstacle
The same penalty applies to everyone in the category or heat
en.narration: If your obstacle has a penalty loop, walk the entire loop yourself. You need to understand the route and the return point, so you can direct an athlete clearly and see whether they complete it. Loops are not all the same. The rulebook says their distance can vary with the terrain, and they can include carries, crawls or other elements. The Head Referee confirms each obstacle's penalty format with the Race Director. Whatever it is, it is applied consistently within the category or heat.
en.review: Under review for 2027: the rulebook (3.17.3) says the penalty is a loop or 30 burpees, as Spartan designates for each obstacle and event. The Officiating SOP says a loop for most obstacles and burpees at the Spear Throw, and the 2026 programme says burpees only at the Spear Throw. Meanwhile, apply the penalty the Head Referee confirms for your obstacle, and contact the Head Referee if you are unsure.

en.heading: Where to stand
points: Choose a spot where you clearly see attempts, completions and failures
Keep your view of the obstacle unobstructed
At the Spear Throw only: set up the camera as the Spear Throw procedure describes
Confirm the camera is recording before the first Elite wave
en.narration: Decide where to stand before the racing starts. You need a position where you can clearly see every attempt, every completion and every failure, with nothing blocking your view. Think about where failures usually happen on your obstacle, and be close enough to speak to an athlete when one does. At the Spear Throw only, you also set up the video camera, following the Spear Throw officiating procedure, and confirm it is recording before the first Elite wave starts. The Head Referee may visit to check enforcement and camera position.

en.heading: In short
points: Attend the mandatory briefing, then reach your obstacle in good time
Know its instructions, failure modes and notes
Inspect the setup, walk the penalty loop, report any concern at once
Stand where you see every attempt; at the Spear Throw, check the camera records
en.narration: In short. Attend the Head Referee's briefing, then get to your obstacle in good time before the first competitive wave. Know its instructions, failure modes and additional notes, including any male and female options. Inspect the setup, walk the penalty loop, and report any doubt or safety concern straight away. Then pick a position where you can see every attempt, and at the Spear Throw, confirm the camera is recording before the first Elite wave.

en.heading: Who you report to
points: Referee, then Head Referee, then Race Director or Timing Team
You report to the Head Referee: the rulebook calls this role the Head Official
The Head Referee is the final authority on enforcing and interpreting the rules
en.narration: The 2026 programme sums up the communication chain in one line: referee, then Head Referee, then the Race Director or the Timing Team. As a referee you report to the Head Referee. The rulebook calls this person the Head Official, and makes them the chief decision maker on all rules matters at the event, and the ultimate authority for enforcing and interpreting the rules. Your reports go to the Head Referee, who passes them on.

en.heading: What the Head Referee passes on
points: Race incidents go to the Race Director, who runs the event's overall operations
Competitor incidents, such as cheating or shortcuts, go to Timing
Confirmed penalties and disqualifications go to the Race Director and Timing
Final penalty decisions may be confirmed by the Head Referee and the timing team
en.narration: The Head Referee links you to the rest of the event. They keep the Race Director, who is responsible for the event's overall operations, informed of race incidents. They tell the Timing team about competitor incidents such as cheating or shortcuts. After video review, they communicate confirmed penalties and disqualifications to the Race Director and the Timing and Tech team. Your job is to enforce the obstacle rules, direct athletes to penalties and record what happened. Final penalty decisions may be confirmed by the Head Referee and the timing team.

en.heading: When to call
points: Join the official channel at check-in: a group chat, a platform or the Head Referee directly
Unsure of a penalty type or how to enforce it: contact the Head Referee at once
Doubts or safety concerns at the obstacle: the Race Director or Head Referee
Hazards: report immediately to the Head Referee, the Race Director or Spartan staff
en.narration: At check-in you join the official communication channel. It might be a WhatsApp group, another messaging platform, or a direct line to the Head Referee. Use it. If you are unsure which penalty applies or how to enforce it, contact the Head Referee immediately rather than guess. Report doubts, safety concerns or inconsistencies at your obstacle to the Race Director or the Head Referee. And report any hazard immediately, to the Head Referee, the Race Director or Spartan staff.

en.heading: Reporting a dispute or an escape
points: Dispute: record the headband number and the reason, and report it as soon as you can
No number: report at once with a clear description, such as clothing and category
Help identify the athlete later on course if asked
No video: write down your penalty decisions and hand them to the Head Referee
en.narration: Most reports are about athletes. If an athlete disputes a call, record their headband number, write down the reason, such as a failed obstacle without the penalty, and report it to the Head Referee as soon as you can. If an athlete leaves without doing the penalty and you can't get their number, report it straight away with a clear description: clothing colour, distinguishing features and race category. Where there is no video, you make penalty decisions on site, write them down and hand them to the Head Referee when you return.

en.heading: In short
points: Your line runs to the Head Referee, who informs the Race Director and Timing
Join the channel at check-in and use it
Ask the Head Referee when unsure, and report hazards immediately
Record headband numbers and reasons, and report disputes and escapes
en.narration: In short. You report to the Head Referee, and the Head Referee informs the Race Director and the Timing team. Join the communication channel at check-in and use it. When you are unsure of a penalty, ask the Head Referee straight away, and report hazards immediately. For disputes and escapes, record the headband number or a clear description, note the reason, and report it.

ocr-4-1.sources: Spartan OCR Rules of Competition 2026: 2.1.5 to 2.1.7, 3.3, 3.17.1, 3.17.2, 3.17.6 to 3.17.8, 4.1.8, 4.2.2, 4.2.13 and 4.3.3. Spartan Referee Online Program 2026: slides 20 to 24 and 44. Officiating SOP 2026: 5.1.2.

en.heading: Three types of obstacle
points: Mandatory: must be completed before the athlete goes on
Multiple attempt (pass/fail): retry until success or the penalty
Single attempt (pass/fail): once committed, complete it or take the penalty
The rulebook's Part D lists each obstacle under one of the three
en.narration: The rulebook splits obstacles into mandatory and pass or fail. Pass or fail obstacles come in two kinds, multiple attempt and single attempt, so in practice you work with three types. A mandatory obstacle must be completed before the athlete goes further. A multiple attempt obstacle can be tried as often as needed, until it is done or a penalty is given. A single attempt obstacle must be completed once the athlete has committed, or the penalty applies. The rulebook lists each obstacle under one type, and the briefing covers the classifications.
en.review: Under review for 2027: the rulebook and the 2026 programme sort several obstacles differently. The rulebook has Monkey Bars, Multi-Rig, Twister, Olympus, Z Wall, Beater and Helix as single attempt, Atlas Carry, Tire Flip and Stairway to Sparta as multiple attempt, and A-Frame Cargo as mandatory. The programme lists the first group as multiple attempt, the second as mandatory and A-Frame Cargo as multiple attempt. Meanwhile, apply the rulebook section for the obstacle and refer a disputed call to the Head Referee.

en.heading: Every obstacle must be attempted
points: At a minimum, an attempt means touching the obstacle
It can include entering water or difficult terrain to reach the obstacle
That terrain can't be bypassed with a penalty unless the briefing or race staff allow it
Failure to attempt an obstacle is a common violation to watch for
en.narration: Every obstacle must be attempted. The rulebook sets the minimum: an attempt is touching the obstacle. Sometimes the attempt also includes getting to the obstacle, for example entering water or crossing other difficult terrain. That terrain can't be skipped by taking a penalty, unless pre-race briefings or race day staff have said it is acceptable. The 2026 programme lists failure to attempt an obstacle among the common rule violations, so watch for athletes who head for the penalty without trying.

en.heading: Mandatory obstacles
points: Completed in full: no bypass and no penalty instead, unless an official says so
Failing one means disqualification; the Race Director may substitute a time penalty
Examples: Bucket Carry, Sandbag Carry, Log Carry, Barbed Wire Crawl
Bucket Carry: material lost means redoing the whole course with a full bucket
en.narration: A mandatory obstacle has to be completed in full before the athlete moves on. The athlete can't bypass it or swap it for a penalty unless a race official instructs them to. Under the rulebook, failing a mandatory obstacle means disqualification, although the Race Director may substitute a time penalty depending on how serious the infraction is. Carries and crawls are typical. At the Bucket Carry, for example, there is no burpee option, and a bucket that comes back with material missing means the athlete redoes the whole course with a correctly filled bucket.

en.heading: Multiple attempt obstacles
points: The athlete may retry as many times as needed
It ends in a completion, or the athlete gives up and takes the penalty
Examples: Rope Climb, Bender, Inverted Wall
Rope Climb: change ropes only after returning to the ground; one rope per attempt
en.narration: A multiple attempt obstacle can be tried again and again. The athlete keeps going until they either complete it or choose to abandon it and take the penalty. Each obstacle's rules say what a retry involves. At the Rope Climb, for example, an athlete may change ropes after returning to the ground and try again, but using more than one rope during a single attempt is a failure. Athletes making repeat attempts should give way to those trying for the first time, although the rulebook says that is not mandatory.

en.heading: Single attempt obstacles: when commitment starts
points: Once committed, the athlete completes the obstacle or takes the penalty: no retry
Each obstacle's own rules define when commitment starts
Spear Throw: when the spear is released in a forward motion
Ape Hanger: when the athlete touches any of the overhead bars
en.narration: A single attempt obstacle gives the athlete one go once they have committed. After that, they either complete it or take the penalty. The key question is when commitment starts, and the rulebook answers it obstacle by obstacle. At the Spear Throw, the attempt starts when the spear is released in a forward motion. At the Ape Hanger, the athlete is committed once they touch any of the overhead bars. Know the commitment point for your obstacle: it decides whether the athlete can still reset.
en.review: Under review for 2027: the 2026 programme says commitment begins once the attempt motion starts, and at the Spear Throw when the spear is drawn back to throw. The rulebook defines commitment obstacle by obstacle, and at the Spear Throw it is on release. Meanwhile, apply each obstacle's rule and refer a disputed call to the Head Referee.

en.heading: What counts as a failure
points: Judge against the failure modes in your obstacle's rules
Kicking a bell with the feet, legs or knees is a failure, with no retry
Failed through significant interference from another athlete: an official may allow a restart
Common failures include using the support structure and not ringing the bell
en.narration: Failure is defined in each obstacle's rules, in its list of failure modes. Judge against that list, not your own idea of how the obstacle should be done. Two general rules apply across obstacles. Kicking a bell with the feet, legs or knees counts as a failure: the athlete can't retry and must complete the penalty. And if significant physical interference from another competitor causes the failure, the athlete may restart with no extra penalty, once an official gives permission.

en.heading: In short
points: Every obstacle must be attempted: at least touching it
Mandatory: complete it in full, or face disqualification
Multiple attempt: retry until done or take the penalty; single attempt: one go once committed
Judge each obstacle's own failure modes; which type is which is under review
en.narration: In short. Every obstacle must be attempted, and touching it is the minimum. A mandatory obstacle must be completed in full, and failing it means disqualification unless the Race Director substitutes a time penalty. A multiple attempt obstacle can be retried until it is done or the athlete takes the penalty. A single attempt obstacle allows one go once the athlete commits, at the point that obstacle's rules define. Judge each obstacle against its own failure modes, and remember that which obstacle is which type is under review for 2027.

ocr-5-1.sources: Spartan OCR Rules of Competition 2026: 3.4.1, 3.4.2, 3.17.1 to 3.17.3, 3.18.1 and 3.18.2. Officiating SOP 2026: 2, 4.1, 5.2.2 to 5.2.4 and 6. Spartan Referee Online Program 2026: slides 17, 26, 29, 33 and 47.

en.heading: Two kinds of obstacle, two kinds of outcome
points: Mandatory obstacles must be completed: failing one means disqualification
The Race Director may substitute a time penalty, depending on how serious it was
Failing a pass/fail obstacle means a penalty: a penalty loop or burpees
en.narration: The rulebook splits obstacles into two categories. Mandatory obstacles must be completed. Failing one means disqualification from the event, although the Race Director may substitute a time penalty, depending on how serious the infraction was. Pass or fail obstacles are different. An athlete who fails one stays in the race and takes a penalty instead. That penalty is either a penalty loop or burpees, and Spartan sets which one applies for each obstacle, event, category or heat.
en.review: Under review for 2027: rule 3.17.3 says the penalty is a penalty loop or 30 burpees, as Spartan designates for each obstacle, event, category or heat, and always 15 burpees at Stadion. The Officiating SOP says a loop for most obstacles and burpees at the Spear Throw; the 2026 programme says burpees only at the Spear Throw. Meanwhile, use the penalty the Head Referee confirms for your obstacle, and ask the Head Referee if you are unsure.

en.heading: The penalty loop
points: A designated stretch of course the athlete completes after failing an obstacle
Its length varies, and it may include carries, crawls or other challenges
It is applied the same way to everyone in the category or heat
Walk the whole loop before racing starts: know the route and the return point
en.narration: A penalty loop is a designated section of course that the athlete completes after failing an obstacle. Its distance can vary with the terrain, and it may include extra challenges such as carries or crawls. Whatever the design, it is applied consistently to everyone in the same category or heat. Before the first competitive wave, walk the entire loop yourself. You need to know the route and the return point, so you can direct athletes correctly and see anyone who cuts it short.

en.heading: Burpee deficits
points: Athletes who don't complete the required burpees have time added to their finish
A large deficit may mean a major time penalty
A shortfall can be found on course or in video review, before the awards
How much time each missed burpee adds is under review for 2027
en.narration: Where burpees are the penalty, an athlete who doesn't complete the required number has time added to their overall finish time. The 2026 programme puts it simply: a large burpee deficit may result in a major time penalty. A shortfall can be found during the race, or in the official video review before the awards, which is why results may not be final straight away. Exactly how much time a missed burpee adds is under review, so this lesson doesn't teach a figure.
en.review: Under review for 2027: rule 3.4.2 adds 30 seconds for each of the first 10 missed burpees and 10 minutes in total if more than 10 are missed. The Officiating SOP adds 30 seconds each and 10 minutes if fewer than 20 are completed; the 2026 programme says 11 or more incorrect is 10 minutes and fewer than 20 is a disqualification. This lesson teaches no figure until the officiating lead rules: the Head Referee confirms penalties.

en.heading: Not completing the penalty
points: Penalty loops must be completed in full
Skipping the penalty brings a further penalty: time added or disqualification
What skipping a loop costs is under review for 2027
Your part: record the headband number and report it to the Head Referee
en.narration: Penalty loops must be completed in full. An athlete who fails a pass or fail obstacle and doesn't complete the penalty has broken the rules, and it will cost them. During the official video review, race officials can add a time penalty or disqualify. The 2026 sources disagree on the exact penalty for skipping a loop, so it is under review. Your part doesn't change: record the athlete's headband number, note what happened, and report it to the Head Referee.
en.review: Under review for 2027: rule 3.4.1 adds a 10-minute time penalty when an athlete fails a pass/fail obstacle and doesn't complete the penalty loop. The 2026 programme says not completing a penalty may result in disqualification, and the Officiating SOP sets no figure. Until the officiating lead rules, apply the rulebook: record it, report it, and leave the penalty to the Head Referee.

en.heading: When an athlete leaves without the penalty
points: Record the headband number and the reason, such as a failed obstacle with no penalty
No number? Give the Head Referee a clear description: clothing, features, category
Report it as soon as you can, and help identify the athlete later if asked
en.narration: The Officiating procedure says what to do when an athlete leaves your obstacle without completing the penalty. Write down their headband number and the reason. Report it to the Head Referee as soon as you operationally can. If you couldn't get the number, report it straight away anyway, with a clear physical description of the athlete: the colour of their clothing, any distinguishing features, and their race category. You may be asked to help identify them later on the course.

en.heading: In short
points: Mandatory obstacle failed: disqualification, unless the Race Director substitutes a time penalty
Pass/fail obstacle failed: a penalty loop, completed in full, or burpees
Missed burpees and skipped loops bring further penalties: the amounts are under review
Record the headband number and report to the Head Referee
en.narration: In short. Fail a mandatory obstacle, and the penalty is disqualification, unless the Race Director substitutes a time penalty. Fail a pass or fail obstacle, and the athlete takes the designated penalty: a penalty loop, completed in full, or burpees. Missed burpees and skipped loops bring further penalties, and the exact amounts are under review for 2027. Whatever happens, record the headband number and report it to the Head Referee.
en.review: Under review for 2027: where burpees are the penalty (rule 3.17.3), the time added for missed burpees (3.4.2) and the penalty for skipping a loop (3.4.1) all differ between the rulebook, the Officiating SOP and the 2026 programme. Until the officiating lead rules, use the penalty the Head Referee confirms for your obstacle, teach no time figure, and refer disputed calls to the Head Referee.

ocr-5-2.sources: Spartan OCR Rules of Competition 2026: 2.1.8, 3.5.1, 3.5.2, 3.6.1, 3.16.1, 3.17.3 and 3.17.6 to 3.17.8. Officiating SOP 2026: 4.1, 5.1.2, 5.2.3 and 5.2.4. Spartan Referee Online Program 2026: slides 18, 27, 28, 35, 36 and 44.

en.heading: Your job at the obstacle
points: Make sure athletes follow the obstacle instructions
Watch for rule violations and know the obstacle's failure conditions
Direct each athlete who fails to the correct penalty
Report issues and non-compliance to the Head Referee
en.narration: The rulebook defines a referee as an official appointed to make sure the rules are followed, usually posted at an obstacle or in the video review tent, and reporting to the Head Official, whom this programme calls the Head Referee. At your obstacle that means four things. Make sure athletes follow the instructions. Watch for violations, knowing exactly what counts as a failure. Send anyone who fails to the correct penalty. And report problems to the Head Referee.

en.heading: Every obstacle must be attempted
points: At a minimum, an attempt means touching the obstacle
It may include entering water or difficult terrain to reach the obstacle
That terrain can't be bypassed with a penalty, unless the briefing or race staff allow it
en.narration: Every obstacle must be attempted. At the very least, an attempt means touching the obstacle. Where the obstacle sits in water or other difficult terrain, the attempt may include getting through that terrain to reach it. Athletes can't bypass that terrain by taking a penalty, unless the pre-race briefing or race day staff have said it is acceptable. So an athlete who walks straight to the penalty without touching the obstacle hasn't met the rule.

en.heading: Bells and interference
points: Bells may only be struck with the arms, hands or body above the chest
Kicking a bell is a failure: no retry, straight to the penalty
Failed because of significant interference from another athlete? An official may allow a restart
en.narration: Two general rules apply at many obstacles. Bells may only be struck with the arms, the hands, or another part of the body above the chest. An athlete who kicks the bell with a foot, leg or knee has failed the obstacle: they can't retry, and they must complete the penalty. And if an athlete fails because another competitor physically interfered in a significant way, an official can give them permission to restart the obstacle with no extra penalty. If you are unsure, ask the Head Referee.

en.heading: Directing to the penalty
points: Send each athlete who fails to the penalty set for your obstacle
Each obstacle's penalty format is confirmed before the event and covered at the briefing
Unsure which penalty applies? Contact the Head Referee straight away
en.narration: When an athlete fails, direct them clearly to the correct penalty. Before the event, the Head Referee confirms the penalty format for each obstacle with the Race Director, whether that is a running loop, a carry loop, a crawl loop or burpees, and the onsite briefing covers what applies to yours. The Officiating procedure says most obstacles use a penalty loop, and the Spear Throw uses burpees. If you are ever unsure which penalty applies, contact the Head Referee immediately.
en.review: Under review for 2027: rule 3.17.3 says the penalty is a penalty loop or 30 burpees, as Spartan designates for each obstacle, event, category or heat, and always 15 burpees at Stadion. The Officiating SOP says a loop for most obstacles and burpees at the Spear Throw; the 2026 programme says burpees only at the Spear Throw. Meanwhile, use the penalty the Head Referee confirms for your obstacle, and ask the Head Referee if you are unsure.

en.heading: Athlete conduct on course
points: Athletes must cover the whole official course: following it is their responsibility
No physical help from anyone but a Spartan official, and no pacing
Being told about other athletes' progress or times isn't assistance
The headband number must be visible and readable at all times
en.narration: Athletes must cover the official course in its entirety, and following it correctly is their own responsibility. They may not accept physical assistance from anyone except a Spartan official. That includes food and drink outside official aid stations, equipment, physical support, and pacing, which means someone running with them to coach them or set the pace. Being told about other athletes' progress or times isn't assistance. The race number on the headband must be plainly displayed and readable at all times.

en.heading: Unsportsmanlike conduct and reporting
points: Athletes must treat everyone with respect: no abusive, threatening or insulting conduct
The Head Referee decides any penalty for conduct: your job is to report it
Record the headband number and what happened, and report to the Head Referee
Explain the rule calmly, and don't escalate a conflict at the obstacle
en.narration: Athletes must treat fellow competitors, Spartan staff, volunteers, spectators and the public with fairness, respect and courtesy, and must not use abusive, threatening or insulting language or behaviour. Unsportsmanlike conduct can lead to a penalty, decided by the Head Official, the Head Referee. Whatever the issue, write down the headband number and what happened, and report it as soon as you can. Reports go from you to the Head Referee, and on to the Race Director or the timing team. If an athlete disputes your call, explain the rule calmly and avoid an argument.

en.heading: In short
points: Every obstacle must be attempted: at a minimum, a touch
Know the failure conditions: a kicked bell is a failure
Send each athlete who fails to your obstacle's penalty; if unsure, ask the Head Referee
Record the number, report to the Head Referee, and don't argue
en.narration: In short. Every obstacle must be attempted, and at a minimum that means touching it. Know the instructions and failure conditions for your obstacle, and the general ones too, such as a kicked bell being a failure. Send each athlete who fails to the penalty set for your obstacle, and ask the Head Referee if you are unsure. Athletes must follow the course, take no outside help, and keep their number visible. When something goes wrong, record the number, report it, and don't argue at the obstacle.

ocr-5-3.sources: Spartan OCR Rules of Competition 2026: 3.4.2, 3.17.3, 3.17.5, 3.18.1 and 4.2.13. Officiating SOP 2026: 4.1, 4.2, 4.2.2, 4.2.3, 5.2.3, 5.2.5 and 6. Spartan Referee Online Program 2026: slide 29.

en.heading: Where burpees are the penalty
points: Spartan designates a loop or burpees for each obstacle, event, category or heat
Where burpees are designated, the penalty is 30 burpees
Stadion events: always 15 burpees
The Spear Throw's penalty is 30 burpees
en.narration: Under rule 3.17.3, the penalty for a pass or fail obstacle is either a penalty loop or burpees, as Spartan designates for each obstacle, event, category or heat. Where burpees are designated, it is thirty burpees. At Stadion events, every obstacle's penalty is fifteen burpees. The Spear Throw's penalty is thirty burpees. Before the event, the Head Referee confirms the penalty format for every obstacle with the Race Director, so the briefing tells you whether your obstacle uses burpees.
en.review: Under review for 2027: rule 3.17.3 says the penalty is a penalty loop or 30 burpees, as Spartan designates for each obstacle, event, category or heat, and always 15 burpees at Stadion. The Officiating SOP says a loop for most obstacles and burpees at the Spear Throw; the 2026 programme says burpees only at the Spear Throw. Meanwhile, use the penalty the Head Referee confirms for your obstacle, and ask the Head Referee if you are unsure.

en.heading: The burpee zone
points: Burpees must be done inside the designated burpee zone
Burpees outside the zone don't count towards the penalty
Officials may add zones when one is full, or to separate categories
Your job: make sure burpees happen in the correct zone
en.narration: Burpees must be completed inside the designated burpee zone. Any done outside it don't count towards the penalty, so an athlete who drifts out of the zone is doing reps that won't be credited. Race officials can designate extra burpee zones when one runs out of room, or to keep categories of athletes apart. Part of your job is to make sure burpees happen in the correct zone, where you and the camera can see them.

en.heading: The headband goes on the ground
points: The athlete places their headband on the ground directly in front of them
Lost headband: record the athlete's name, or say it on the camera's audio
Tell the Head Referee about any athlete recorded without a headband
en.narration: While doing burpees, the athlete places their headband on the ground directly in front of them. The Head Referee's start-line announcements cover this, so athletes should know it before they reach you. If an athlete has lost their headband, record their name, or use the camera's audio to say who they are. Either way, tell the Head Referee about any athlete recorded without a headband, so the footage can be matched to the right person.

en.heading: Showing the athlete to the camera
points: Hold the headband about two feet from the lens for about two seconds
Give it straight back to the athlete
Never hold two headbands at once, and don't let athletes hand them to you
Never move an athlete's body or face to suit the camera
en.narration: At the Spear Throw, the video identifies each athlete. Hold the headband about two feet from the camera lens for about two seconds, so the number is clear on review. Then return it to the athlete immediately. Never hold two headbands at the same time, and don't let athletes hand their headbands to you. And never physically move an athlete's body or face to get them in shot: identification comes from the headband, held up clearly.

en.heading: Video review determines missed burpees
points: Missed burpees are determined in video review
Results may not be final until the official video review is done
Footage stays with the Head Referee and is never given to athletes
Your three jobs: the movement standard, the zone, a clear identification
en.narration: The 2026 programme says video review determines missed burpees. That is why results may not be posted straight away: the official review happens before they are final. The Head Referee manages the review as referees return from their obstacles, keeps the footage until the end of the event day, and never gives it to athletes. Your part on the course is what makes the review possible: enforce the movement standard, keep burpees in the zone, and identify each athlete clearly for the camera.
en.review: Under review for 2027: the time added for missed burpees differs between rule 3.4.2, the Officiating SOP and the 2026 programme, and the SOP lets the referee on site decide, in writing, where there is no video. The lesson on burpee time penalties sets out each version. This lesson teaches no figure: the Head Referee confirms penalties after review.

en.heading: In short
points: Burpees are the penalty where Spartan designates them: 30, or 15 at Stadion
Only burpees inside the zone count
Headband on the ground in front; shown to the camera, then straight back
Video review determines missed burpees
en.narration: In short. Burpees are the penalty where Spartan designates them: thirty burpees, or fifteen at Stadion events, and always at the Spear Throw. Only burpees inside the designated zone count. The athlete's headband goes on the ground in front of them, and you show it to the camera for a couple of seconds, then give it straight back. Video review then determines any missed burpees, so your job is the standard, the zone and a clear identification.
en.review: Under review for 2027: rule 3.17.3 says the penalty is a penalty loop or 30 burpees, as Spartan designates for each obstacle, event, category or heat, and always 15 burpees at Stadion. The Officiating SOP says a loop for most obstacles and burpees at the Spear Throw; the 2026 programme says burpees only at the Spear Throw. Meanwhile, use the penalty the Head Referee confirms for your obstacle, and ask the Head Referee if you are unsure.

ocr-6-1.sources: Spartan OCR Rules of Competition 2026: 3.17.4. Spartan Referee Online Program 2026: slides 31, 44 and 46.

en.heading: One complete burpee
points: One cycle between two positions: the bottom and the top
From the bottom position up to the top, then a jump
A rep that misses part of the standard isn't a complete burpee
en.narration: Rule 3.17.4 defines one complete burpee. It is one cycle between two body positions, called the top and the bottom. The athlete moves from the bottom position up to the top position, and then jumps. Every rep in a burpee penalty has to meet this standard. A rep that misses part of it isn't a complete burpee, and you can require the athlete to do another. The next slides take each part in turn.

en.heading: The bottom and the top
points: Bottom: lying prone on the ground, with the chest touching the ground
Top: balanced and upright, a stance anyone could hold without falling over
At the top, the hips and knees are extended, not bent
en.narration: The bottom position is lying prone, face down on the ground, with the chest touching the ground. The top position is a balanced, upright standing position: one that anyone could hold for a long time without falling forwards or backwards. At the top, the athlete's hips and knees should be extended, not bent. Watch both ends of every rep. A chest that stops short of the ground, or hips still bent at the top, means the rep hasn't met the standard.

en.heading: The jump
points: Once back at the top, the athlete jumps
The hands are extended upwards, above the ears
No jump, or hands not above the ears: the rep isn't complete
en.narration: Once the athlete has returned to the top position from the bottom, they jump, with their hands extended upwards above their ears. The rule puts the jump after the top position is reached, so the athlete needs to stand upright first. Watch the hands as well as the feet. Hands that only reach the shoulders or the face don't meet the standard, and neither does a rep with no jump at all.

en.heading: One continuous movement
points: The 2026 programme: the movement must be continuous for each rep
Fast reps still have to meet every part of the standard
A typical fault: fast burpees with incomplete extension at the top
en.narration: The 2026 programme adds that the movement must be continuous for each rep: down to the ground, up to standing, and the jump, as one movement. It also gives a typical scenario to watch for: an athlete doing fast burpees without fully extending at the top. The question is always the same. Did the rep meet the standard? Chest on the ground, hips and knees extended at the top, then a jump with the hands above the ears. If not, it isn't a complete burpee.

en.heading: In short
points: Bottom: lying prone, chest touching the ground
Top: balanced and upright, hips and knees extended
Then a jump with the hands above the ears
One continuous movement, and every rep to the standard, however fast
en.narration: In short. One complete burpee goes from the bottom position to the top position, followed by a jump. At the bottom, the athlete lies prone with the chest touching the ground. At the top, they stand balanced and upright, with the hips and knees extended. Then they jump with the hands above the ears. Each rep is one continuous movement, and every rep has to meet the standard, however fast it is done.

ocr-6-2.sources: Spartan OCR Rules of Competition 2026: 3.17.4 and 3.17.5. Officiating SOP 2026: 5.2.4, 5.2.5 and 6. Spartan Referee Online Program 2026: slides 32, 35, 36, 43 and 46.

en.heading: Athletes count, you don't
points: Athletes count their own burpees
Referees don't count for them
Your job is the standard: watch every rep
Remind athletes that the movement and the reps are being monitored
en.narration: Athletes are responsible for counting their own burpees. Referees do not count for them. That leaves you free for the job that matters: watching whether each rep meets the movement standard. The 2026 programme suggests reminding athletes that both the movement standard and the number of reps are being monitored. Where there is video, the number and the quality of the burpees are checked again in the video review.

en.heading: Watching the standard
points: Stand where your view of the athlete is unobstructed
Check the chest at the bottom, the hips and knees at the top, the hands in the jump
Keep the burpees inside the zone, with the headband on the ground in front
Don't touch or move the athlete for the camera
en.narration: Position yourself so your view is unobstructed. You need to see the chest reach the ground, the hips and knees extend at the top, and the hands go above the ears in the jump. Keep an eye on the zone as well, because burpees outside it don't count, and on the headband, which stays on the ground in front of the athlete. Never physically move an athlete's body or face to suit the camera.

en.heading: Asking for extra burpees
points: A rep below the standard: require an extra burpee
Explain clearly and calmly what was missing
Exhausted athletes may continue if their effort is genuine
en.narration: When a rep doesn't meet the standard, require the athlete to do extra burpees, so the penalty is made up of complete burpees. Explain clearly and calmly what was missing, for example the chest not touching the ground, or the hips still bent at the top. Some athletes will be exhausted. The 2026 programme says to let them continue if their effort is genuine. They can keep going, but each rep still has to meet the standard.

en.heading: When an athlete disputes your call
points: Stay calm, explain the rule, and avoid an argument
Record the headband number and what was disputed
Refer the dispute to the Head Referee
Don't escalate a conflict at the obstacle
en.narration: Some athletes will disagree when you ask for extra burpees. Stay calm and professional, explain the rule clearly, and don't get drawn into an argument. Record the athlete's headband number and what was disputed, and report it to the Head Referee as soon as you can. Disputes are the Head Referee's to resolve, not yours to win at the obstacle. Keep watching the other athletes in the zone while you deal with it.

en.heading: In short
points: Athletes count; you watch the standard
Clear view of the chest, the hips and knees, and the hands
Below the standard: require extra burpees, explained calmly
Exhausted but genuine: let them continue; disputes go to the Head Referee
en.narration: In short. Athletes count their own burpees, and you watch the standard. Stand where you can clearly see the chest at the bottom, the hips and knees at the top, and the hands in the jump, and keep the burpees inside the zone. If a rep falls short, require extra burpees and explain why, calmly. Let exhausted athletes continue if their effort is genuine. And if an athlete disputes your call, record the number and refer it to the Head Referee.

ocr-6-3.sources: Spartan OCR Rules of Competition 2026: 3.4.2, 3.17.4, 3.17.5 and 3.18.1 to 3.18.3. Officiating SOP 2026: 4.2.2 and 6. Spartan Referee Online Program 2026: slides 29 and 33.

en.heading: Missed burpees become time
points: Athletes who don't complete the required burpees have time added to their finish
Shortfalls are found on course or in the review before the awards
How much time is added is under review for 2027
en.narration: Where burpees are the penalty and an athlete doesn't complete the required number, time is added to their overall finish time. Missed burpees can be identified during the race, or in the post-race review before the awards. All three 2026 sources agree that missed burpees cost time. They don't agree on how much, so this lesson doesn't teach a figure. The amounts are under review for 2027, until the officiating lead rules.
en.review: Under review for 2027: rule 3.4.2 adds 30 seconds for each of the first 10 missed burpees and 10 minutes in total if more than 10 are missed. The Officiating SOP adds 30 seconds each and 10 minutes if fewer than 20 are completed; the 2026 programme says 11 or more incorrect is 10 minutes and fewer than 20 is a disqualification. This lesson teaches no figure until the officiating lead rules: the Head Referee confirms penalties.

en.heading: Where the 2026 sources disagree
points: How much time each missed burpee adds, and whether there is a ceiling
Where the threshold sits: burpees missed, or burpees completed
Whether a large shortfall means a time penalty or disqualification
Stadion, with its 15-burpee penalty, is disputed too
en.narration: The rulebook, the Officiating procedure and the 2026 programme each describe burpee time penalties differently. They differ on how much time a missed burpee adds, and whether there is a ceiling. They differ on where the threshold sits, counted in burpees missed or in burpees completed. And they differ on whether a large shortfall means a long time penalty or disqualification. Stadion, where the penalty is fifteen burpees, has the same problem. Until the officiating lead rules, treat every figure as under review.
en.review: Under review for 2027: rule 3.4.2 adds 30 seconds for each of the first 10 missed burpees and 10 minutes in total for more than 10 (Stadion: 30 seconds each for the first 5, 5 minutes for more than 5). The Officiating SOP adds 30 seconds per missed burpee and 10 minutes if fewer than 20 are completed (Stadion: fewer than 10). The 2026 programme says 30 seconds each, 10 minutes for 11 or more incorrect, and disqualification for fewer than 20. Meanwhile, quote no figure to athletes: refer questions about time penalties to the Head Referee.

en.heading: What counts as a missed burpee
points: A burpee that wasn't done
A burpee outside the designated zone: it doesn't count towards the penalty
A rep below the movement standard: it isn't a complete burpee
Review looks at both the number and the quality of the burpees
en.narration: A shortfall isn't only burpees that were never done. Burpees done outside the designated zone don't count towards the penalty. A rep that doesn't meet the movement standard isn't a complete burpee, and the 2026 programme treats missed and incorrect burpees alike. Under the Officiating procedure, the review decides on both the quantity and the quality of the burpees. That is why enforcing the standard on the spot, and asking for extra reps, matters.
en.review: Under review for 2027: how much time missed or incorrect burpees add differs between rule 3.4.2, the Officiating SOP and the 2026 programme. What counts as a complete burpee does not: apply rules 3.17.4 and 3.17.5, and leave the time penalty to the Head Referee.

en.heading: Who decides the penalty
points: With video: burpee decisions on number and quality are made in video review
Without video: you decide on site, write it down, and give it to the Head Referee
The Head Referee sends confirmed penalties to the Race Director and the timing team
Penalties are shown in the results tent during the review
en.narration: Where there is video, decisions on how many burpees were done, and how well, are made in the video review. The Head Referee manages that review as referees return from their obstacles, and sends confirmed penalties and disqualifications to the Race Director and the timing team. Where there is no video, the Officiating procedure says the referee on site decides, documents the decision in writing, and gives it to the Head Referee on returning from the obstacle. Penalties are shown in the results tent during the review.
en.review: Under review for 2027: the Officiating SOP (6.iii) says burpee penalty decisions are made in video review where there is video, and by the referee on site, in writing, where there isn't. The 2026 programme says penalty decisions are made by the video review team. Meanwhile, follow the Officiating SOP: with no camera, write your decision down and give it to the Head Referee.

en.heading: In short
points: Missed or incorrect burpees add time to the athlete's finish
How much time is under review for 2027: refer questions to the Head Referee
Enforce the standard and the zone on the spot
With video, review decides; without it, write your decision down
en.narration: In short. Missed or incorrect burpees add time to the athlete's finish, but how much time is under review for 2027, because the rulebook, the Officiating procedure and the 2026 programme disagree. Don't quote a figure: refer questions to the Head Referee. What you control is on the course: the movement standard and the zone. Where there is video, the review decides. Where there isn't, write your decision down and give it to the Head Referee.
en.review: Under review for 2027: the time added for missed burpees differs between rule 3.4.2, the Officiating SOP and the 2026 programme (each version is on the second slide), and the SOP and the programme differ on who decides when there is no video. Until the officiating lead rules, teach no figure, follow the Officiating SOP on written decisions, and refer disputed calls to the Head Referee.

ocr-7-1.sources: Spartan OCR Rules of Competition 2026: 3.5.1, 3.5.2, 3.6.1, 3.11.1, 3.18.1, 3.18.4, 3.19.1 and 3.19.3. Officiating SOP 2026: 4.2, 4.2.3 and 5.2.4. Spartan Referee Online Program 2026: slides 28, 35 and 36.

en.heading: Answering an athlete's question
points: Stay calm and professional, whatever the tone of the question
Explain the rule clearly: what the obstacle asked for, and what was missed
Avoid arguments: a question isn't a debate
en.narration: Athletes will ask you about your calls, often while they are tired and frustrated. Stay calm and professional. Answer by explaining the rule clearly: what the obstacle asked of them, and which part they didn't meet. Keep it short, because other athletes are still arriving at your obstacle. If the athlete accepts the explanation, send them to the penalty. If they don't, it has become a dispute. You don't settle a dispute by arguing at the obstacle. You refer it to the Head Referee.

en.heading: When it becomes a dispute
points: Record the athlete's headband number
Write down the reason, for example a failed obstacle with no penalty completed
Report it to the Head Referee as soon as you can
Don't escalate the conflict at the obstacle
en.narration: If an athlete disputes your call, you have three jobs. First, record their headband number. The rules make every competitor responsible for keeping their race number on their headband, readable, at all times. Second, write down the reason for the dispute, for example that the athlete failed the obstacle and did not complete the penalty. Third, report it to the Head Referee as soon as you operationally can. The decision isn't made at your obstacle, so there is nothing to gain by escalating. Keep your notes factual: the Head Referee will rely on them.

en.heading: When you can't get the headband number
points: Report it to the Head Referee straight away
Give a clear description: clothing colour, distinguishing features, race category
Help identify the athlete later on course if you are asked
en.narration: Sometimes an athlete leaves the obstacle area without completing the penalty, and you can't read their number. The officiating procedure covers this. Report it to the Head Referee immediately, rather than waiting until you come back from the obstacle. Give a clear physical description: the colour of their clothing, anything that makes them easy to recognise, and their race category if you can tell. You may be asked to help identify the athlete later on the course. Meanwhile, stay focused on your obstacle and the athletes still arriving.

en.heading: Athlete conduct
points: Athletes must treat officials with fairness, respect and courtesy
Abusive, threatening or insulting language or conduct breaks the rules
The Head Official decides any penalty for a conduct violation
Your part: record the number, note what happened, report it
en.narration: The rules expect athletes to treat everyone at the event, officials included, with fairness, respect and courtesy, and not to use abusive, threatening or insulting language or conduct. A conduct violation can lead to a penalty that depends on how serious it was. In the rulebook, that decision belongs to the Head Official, not to you. Gross unsportsmanlike conduct, or physical violence towards an official, can be grounds for suspension. Your part is the same as in any dispute: stay calm, record the headband number, note what was said or done, and report it to the Head Referee.

en.heading: After the race: protests and video review
points: Results aren't final until the official video review has taken place
Athletes bring protests to the Head Official during the protest period
Officials don't have to consider footage taken by athletes or spectators
Official video footage is never given to competitors
en.narration: A disputed call doesn't end at your obstacle. Before results are final, there is an official video review. An athlete who wants to challenge a penalty brings a protest to the Head Official during the protest period, which starts as soon as they cross the finish line. Officials are not obliged to consider videos or photos taken by competitors or spectators. The officiating procedure also says official footage is never given to competitors. So if an athlete offers you their phone footage, or asks to see yours, point them to the Head Referee and the protest process.
en.review: Under review for 2027: Rule 3.19.1 ends the protest period 15 minutes before the award ceremony for the athlete's category. The Officiating SOP gives half an hour before the awards as an example, and lets referee errors for non-podium athletes be corrected up to two hours after the final awards. Meanwhile, apply the rulebook and refer timing questions to the Head Referee.
