en.heading: In short
points: Stay calm, explain the rule clearly, don't argue
Dispute: headband number, what happened, report to the Head Referee
No number: report at once, with a clear description
Protests and video review happen after the race, not at your obstacle
en.narration: In short. Answer questions calmly and explain the rule clearly, without arguing. If it becomes a dispute, record the headband number, write down what happened, and report it to the Head Referee as soon as you can. If you can't get the number, report it at once with a clear description of the athlete. Abusive conduct is recorded and reported the same way. The final decision comes later, through the video review and the protest period, not at your obstacle.

ocr-8-1.sources: Spartan OCR Rules of Competition 2026: 1.2.1, 2.1.2, 2.1.3, 2.1.8, 3.2 and 3.18.2. Officiating SOP 2026: 1, 4.2, 4.2.2, 5.2.3 and 6.iii. Spartan Referee Online Program 2026: slides 12, 18, 38 and 39.

en.heading: Professional conduct at your obstacle
points: Stay focused on your obstacle
Avoid distractions and extended conversations
Remain neutral and respectful with every athlete
Represent Spartan professionally
en.narration: The rules exist so that every Spartan event is run fairly and consistently, in a spirit of sportsmanship and integrity. At your obstacle, you are how that happens. Stay focused on the obstacle and the athletes attempting it. Avoid distractions and extended conversations, because a failure you didn't see is a failure you can't call. Remain neutral and respectful with everyone, whoever they are. To athletes and spectators, you are Spartan, so represent Spartan professionally.

en.heading: Where a referee sits in the rules
points: A referee is a Spartan-appointed official who makes sure the rules are followed
Usually posted at an obstacle or in the video review tent
The Head Official is the chief decision maker and final authority on the rules
Your chain: you, the Head Referee, then the Race Director or Timing Team
en.narration: The rulebook defines a referee as a Spartan-appointed official whose task is to make sure the rules are followed, usually posted at obstacles or in the video review tent. Referees report to the Head Official, who is the chief decision maker on all matters of the rules at an event, and the ultimate authority for enforcing and interpreting them. In the officiating procedure and this programme, you report to the Head Referee. The Head Referee then reports race incidents to the Race Director, and penalties to the Timing Team.

en.heading: What you decide
points: Enforce the obstacle rules
Direct athletes who fail to the correct penalty
Document violations
Unsure of the penalty or how to enforce it? Contact the Head Referee at once
en.narration: At your obstacle, you are responsible for three things. You enforce the obstacle's rules. You direct an athlete who fails to the correct penalty for that obstacle. And you document violations. Where there is no video evidence of burpees, the officiating procedure makes the decision on burpee quantity and quality yours: you make it on site, write it down, and hand it to the Head Referee when you return. If you are unsure about the penalty type or how to enforce it, contact the Head Referee straight away.

en.heading: Who confirms a penalty
points: Final penalty decisions may be confirmed by the Head Referee and the timing team
In video review, officials can still assess penalties, up to disqualification
The Head Referee passes confirmed penalties to the Race Director and Timing
Your notes are the evidence those decisions rest on
en.narration: Your call starts the process, but it isn't always the last word. The programme says final penalty decisions may be confirmed by the Head Referee and the timing team. Under the rulebook, the Head Official is ultimately responsible for upholding the rules, and during the official video review, race officials can still assess penalties, including disqualification. The Head Referee manages that review, and passes confirmed penalties and disqualifications to the Race Director and the Timing Team. That is why your notes matter: clear, factual records let the right decision be confirmed.

en.heading: In short
points: Focused, neutral, respectful and professional
You enforce the rules, direct athletes to penalties and document violations
The Head Referee confirms penalties and handles what you refer
Unsure? Contact the Head Referee straight away
en.narration: In short. Stay focused on your obstacle, neutral and respectful, and represent Spartan professionally. You enforce the obstacle rules, direct athletes who fail to the correct penalty, and document violations. The Head Official has final authority on the rules, and the Head Referee confirms penalties, handles what you refer, and passes them on to the Race Director and Timing. If you are ever unsure, contact the Head Referee straight away.

ocr-8-2.sources: Spartan OCR Rules of Competition 2026: 1.2.1, 3.2, 3.6.1, 3.17.3, 4.1.6, 4.1.8 and 4.3.9. Officiating SOP 2026: 5.2.2 and 5.2.3. Spartan Referee Online Program 2026: slides 11, 12, 17, 40 and 41.

en.heading: Safety is part of the job
points: The rules aim to protect athletes' health, safety and well-being
Monitor your obstacle's safety, and make sure athletes move safely
Don't allow dangerous shortcuts: athletes must cover the whole official course
en.narration: One purpose of the rules is to protect the health, safety and well-being of competitors, as far as that can reasonably be achieved in obstacle course racing. The programme puts athlete safety alongside fairness as your priority. That means monitoring the safety of your obstacle, making sure athletes move safely, and not allowing dangerous shortcuts. A shortcut is never yours to allow: the rules require athletes to cover the official course in its entirety.

en.heading: Inspect, and report hazards at once
points: Before the first wave, inspect the setup and check it is serviceable
Walk the penalty loop and learn the athletes' approach direction
Report hazards immediately: Head Referee, Race Director or Spartan staff
en.narration: Safety starts before the first competitive wave. When you arrive at your obstacle, inspect the setup and check that it is serviceable. Review the race flow and the direction athletes will approach from, and walk the whole penalty loop so you know its route and its return point. If anything worries you, a doubt, a safety concern or an inconsistency, report it immediately to the Head Referee or the Race Director. During the race, report any hazard straight away to the Head Referee, the Race Director or Spartan staff.

en.heading: Safe movement in the obstacle rules
points: Rope Climb: come down safely and under control, at least one hand on the rope
Hercules Hoist: lower the weight under control; dropping it is a failure
Swim or water crossing: no diving; diving is a failure
en.narration: Some obstacle rules build safety in directly, and you enforce them like any other rule. At the Rope Climb, athletes must return to the ground in a safe and controlled manner, with at least one hand touching the rope at all times. At the Hercules Hoist, the weight must be lowered under control, not in freefall, and dropping it in an uncontrolled manner is a failure. At a swim or water crossing, diving isn't allowed, and it is a failure mode. Know your obstacle's safety rules before the first athlete arrives.

en.heading: The same interpretation all race
points: Apply the rules equally to all athletes
Use the same interpretation from the first wave to the last
Each penalty applies consistently within its category or heat
Your focus: the Competitive categories, Elite and Age Group
en.narration: Consistency is what makes results fair. Apply the rules equally to every athlete, and use the same interpretation from the first wave to the last. The call you make for the first Elite athlete is the standard for everyone after them. The rulebook says each penalty is applied consistently within the designated category or heat. Your focus is the Competitive categories, Elite and Age Group, who are expected to follow every rule. Open racers are encouraged to follow the rules too, in a more relaxed atmosphere.

en.heading: Stick to the rule, and escalate when unsure
points: Judge against the obstacle's written failure modes
Avoid personal judgement beyond the rule
When unsure, escalate the decision to the Head Referee
en.narration: Consistency also means not adding rules of your own. Judge each attempt against the obstacle's written failure modes, not against what you personally think is fair, and avoid judgement beyond what the rule says. If a situation isn't clearly covered, or you are unsure which penalty applies or how to enforce it, contact the Head Referee straight away. A decision escalated and made once can then be applied the same way to everyone.

en.heading: In short
points: Monitor safety, insist on safe movement, allow no shortcuts
Inspect early and report hazards at once
Same rules, same interpretation, every athlete, all race
Unsure? Escalate to the Head Referee
en.narration: In short. Athlete safety sits alongside fairness as your priority. Monitor your obstacle, make sure athletes move safely, and allow no shortcuts. Inspect the obstacle and walk the penalty loop before the first wave, and report hazards straight away to the Head Referee, the Race Director or Spartan staff. Apply the same rules, with the same interpretation, to every athlete all race. And when you are unsure, escalate to the Head Referee.

ocr-9-1.sources: Spartan OCR Rules of Competition 2026: 3.17.7, 4.2.6, 4.2.7, 4.2.8, 4.2.10 and 4.2.17. Officiating SOP 2026: 2 and 5.2.2. Spartan Referee Online Program 2026: slides 17 and 43.

en.heading: Watch the hands and feet
points: Most failure modes are about what the hands and feet touch
Monkey Bars: hands and arms only; feet or legs on the bars is a failure
Olympus: feet may rest on the wall, but a foot on a hold or hole is a failure
en.narration: Most obstacle failures come down to what an athlete's hands and feet are touching, so that is where your eyes go. At the Monkey Bars, the athlete traverses using only hands and arms. Feet or legs touching the bars is a failure, and so is touching the ground to create an advantage. At Olympus, athletes may put their feet and knees against the wall for support, but touching any hold or hole with the feet is a failure. Know exactly which contacts your obstacle allows.

en.heading: Focus on the exact rule
points: Know your obstacle's instructions, failure modes and notes before the first wave
Helix and Z Wall: the attempt starts at four points of contact
Monkey Bars, Multi-Rig, Olympus: once both feet leave the starting step
en.narration: Each obstacle has its own rule, with competitor instructions, failure modes and additional notes. Watch for that rule, not a general idea of a good attempt. Know when the attempt starts, because from then on the athlete is committed. At the Helix and the Z Wall, it starts once four points of contact are made. At the Monkey Bars, the Multi-Rig and Olympus, it starts once both feet have left the starting step. If you miss the start, you can't be sure what counts.

en.heading: Where to stand
points: A spot with an unobstructed view of attempts, completions and failures
Check the race flow and the athletes' approach direction
Anticipate where failures usually happen, and keep those points in view
en.narration: Before the first wave, work out the best place to stand. You need an unobstructed view of the attempts, the completions and the failures. Review the race flow and the direction athletes approach from. Think about where failures usually occur on your obstacle, and make sure those points are in clear view. The officiating procedure calls obstacles with a history of frequent failures high-failure obstacles. They need active enforcement, so your position there matters even more.

en.heading: Ready to engage on a failure
points: Stand where you can speak to a failing athlete and direct them to the penalty
Know the penalty loop's route and return point
Keep the bell in view: kicking it is a failure
en.narration: Seeing a failure is half the job. The other half is engaging the athlete, so position yourself where you can speak to them as soon as they fail and point them to the penalty. Walk the penalty loop beforehand, so you know its route and where it returns to the course. Keep the bell in view too. Under the general rule, bells may only be struck with the arms, the hands or another part of the body above the chest. Kicking the bell is a failure. Check your obstacle's own rule as well.

en.heading: In short
points: Watch the hands and feet
Know the exact rule, and when the attempt starts
Stand with a clear view of where failures happen
Be ready to direct the athlete to the penalty
en.narration: In short. Watch the athlete's hands and feet, because that is where most failures happen. Know the exact rule for your obstacle, including the moment the attempt starts. Stand where your view is unobstructed and the usual failure points are in sight. And position yourself so you can engage the athlete as soon as they fail, and send them on the right penalty.

ocr-9-2.sources: Spartan OCR Rules of Competition 2026: 2.1.10, 3.4.1, 3.17.4 to 3.17.7, 4.1.1, 4.2.6, 4.2.7, 4.2.8 and 4.2.10. Spartan Referee Online Program 2026: slides 26, 31, 32 and 44.

en.heading: Using the support structure
points: Walls: using the support structure, sides or straps is a failure
Rigs: using vertical truss as a ladder is a failure
Horizontal truss may be used to start or transfer, where the rule allows it
en.narration: The truss is the obstacle's main supporting structure: the metal diagonal, vertical and horizontal beams. Many obstacles forbid using it. At the walls, using the support structure, the sides of the wall or the straps to help with balance, climbing up or coming down is a failure. On the Monkey Bars and other rigs, using vertical truss as a ladder to start, traverse or finish is a failure. But many rigs let athletes use horizontal truss to start, or to transfer during the traverse. Check which applies to your obstacle.

en.heading: Handling outside the permitted area
points: Multi-Rig: grabbing the ropes, slings or chains holding an attachment is a failure
Helix: using bars from another lane is a failure
Olympus: touching a hold or hole with the feet is a failure
en.narration: Handling outside the permitted area means using a part of the obstacle the rule doesn't allow. At the Multi-Rig, athletes may use only the attachments. Grabbing the ropes, slings or chains that fix them to the structure is a failure, and so is using more than one lane. At the Helix, using bars from another lane is a failure. At Olympus, the hands work the holds, and a foot on a hold or hole is a failure. Know your obstacle's permitted area exactly.

en.heading: Not attempting, and skipping the loop
points: Every obstacle must be attempted: at a minimum, the athlete touches it
An athlete who fails must complete the penalty loop in full
Skipping the loop is penalised: the penalty is under review for 2027
en.narration: Every obstacle must be attempted. At a minimum, an attempt means touching the obstacle. Sometimes it means getting through water or difficult terrain to reach it, and that can't be bypassed with a penalty unless the briefing or race staff say so. An athlete who attempts and fails must complete the penalty loop in full. Skipping it is a violation that you record and report to the Head Referee. The sources differ on the penalty for it, so it is under review.
en.review: Under review for 2027: Rule 3.4.1 adds a 10-minute time penalty when an athlete doesn't complete the penalty loop. The 2026 online programme says it may result in disqualification. Meanwhile, apply the rulebook and refer the case to the Head Referee.

en.heading: Burpees that don't meet the standard
points: Chest to the ground, upright with hips and knees extended, then a jump, hands above ears
Burpees outside the designated burpee zone don't count
Athletes count their own burpees: you don't count for them
en.narration: Improper burpees are one of the most common violations. One complete burpee goes from the bottom position, lying with the chest on the ground, to a balanced upright position with hips and knees extended, followed by a jump with the hands above the ears. Burpees done outside the designated zone don't count. Athletes count their own burpees, and you don't count for them. Where the standard isn't met, the programme says to require extra burpees, and to remind the athlete that their movement and their reps are being monitored.

en.heading: The bell
points: On rigs such as the Monkey Bars, failing to ring the bell is a failure
Bells may be struck with the arms, hands or body above the chest
Kicking the bell is a failure: no retry, the athlete takes the penalty
en.narration: Many obstacles finish at a bell, and on rigs such as the Monkey Bars, failure to ring it is a failure mode. An athlete who comes off before ringing the bell has failed, however far they got. Under the general rule, bells may only be struck with the arms and hands, or another part of the body above the chest. Using the feet, legs or knees to kick the bell counts as an obstacle failure. The athlete may not retry, and must complete the penalty for that obstacle.

en.heading: In short
points: No support structure or vertical truss unless the rule allows it
Only the permitted parts of the obstacle, in one lane
Attempt every obstacle, and complete every penalty loop in full
Burpees to the standard, in the zone; bells rung, never kicked
en.narration: In short. Watch for athletes using the support structure, or vertical truss as a ladder, where the rule forbids it. Watch for handling outside the permitted area, such as grabbing the ropes or chains on a rig, or using another lane. Every obstacle must be attempted, and every penalty loop completed in full. Burpees must meet the standard and be done in the zone. And the bell must be rung, never kicked.

ocr-9-3.sources: Spartan OCR Rules of Competition 2026: 3.4.1, 3.17.4, 4.2.6, 4.2.7, 4.2.10 and 4.2.17. Officiating SOP 2026: 5.2.4 and 6.iii. Spartan Referee Online Program 2026: slides 12, 32, 33 and 45 to 47.

en.heading: How to decide
points: Find the exact rule: instructions, failure modes and notes
Check whether what you saw matches a listed failure mode
Make the call, direct the athlete, record it, and escalate when unsure
en.narration: This lesson gives you three situations from the 2026 programme. For each one, decide what you would do before you hear the answer. The method is the same every time. Find the exact rule for the obstacle. Check whether what you saw matches one of its listed failure modes. Then make the call, direct the athlete, and record what happened. If the rule doesn't settle it, or you are unsure, escalate to the Head Referee.

en.heading: Scenario 1: a brief touch on the top
points: An athlete on the Helix briefly touches the top of the obstacle with one hand
The touch lasts a moment and gives them no advantage
They carry on and ring the bell
en.narration: Rule 4.2.6 lists touching the top of the Helix as a failure mode, with no condition about advantage. Olympus and the Z Wall are the same. So the call the rulebook supports is a failure, and the athlete takes the penalty, even though the touch gained nothing. Advantage matters where the rule says so. At the Monkey Bars, under rule 4.2.7, feet touching the ground is a failure when it creates an advantage. Always check the wording of the failure mode before you decide.
en.review: Under review for 2027: the 2026 online programme asks referees to consider whether the touch created an advantage, and to focus on rule intent, not minor accidental contact. Rules 4.2.6, 4.2.10 and 4.2.17 list touching the top as a failure with no advantage test. Meanwhile, apply the rulebook and refer a disputed call to the Head Referee.

en.heading: Scenario 2: fast burpees, hips not extended
points: An athlete is doing their penalty burpees after failing the Spear Throw
They are moving fast, and at the top of many reps their hips are still bent
en.narration: Those reps don't meet the standard. Rule 3.17.4 defines the top position as balanced and upright, with the hips and knees extended, not bent, before the jump. A rep without it isn't a complete burpee. The programme says to require extra burpees when the standard isn't met, and to remind the athlete that their movement and reps are being monitored. Don't count for them. At the Spear Throw, the video review team decides missed burpees. Without video, you decide on site, write it down and give it to the Head Referee.
en.review: Under review for 2027: the time added for missed or incorrect burpees differs between the rulebook (3.4.2), the Officiating SOP and the 2026 programme. This lesson doesn't teach a figure until the officiating lead rules.

en.heading: Scenario 3: running past the penalty loop
points: An athlete fails a pass/fail obstacle at your station
You direct them to the penalty loop, but they run straight past it and carry on
en.narration: This is a clear violation. Under rule 3.4.1, an athlete who attempts and fails a pass or fail obstacle must complete the penalty loop, and this one didn't. Don't chase them or argue. Record the headband number, document what happened, and report it to the Head Referee as soon as you can. If you couldn't read the number, report it immediately with a clear description: clothing colour, distinguishing features and race category. The penalty itself is decided through the Head Referee, not at your obstacle.
en.review: Under review for 2027: Rule 3.4.1 adds a 10-minute time penalty when the penalty loop isn't completed. The 2026 online programme says it may result in disqualification. Meanwhile, apply the rulebook and refer the case to the Head Referee.

en.heading: In short
points: Read the failure mode's exact wording: advantage counts only where it says so
A burpee without full extension at the top doesn't count
A skipped penalty loop: record the number, document, report
Unsure? Escalate to the Head Referee
en.narration: In short. A brief touch on the top of the Helix, Olympus or the Z Wall is a failure under the rulebook, because the failure mode has no advantage test, while some other failure modes do. A burpee without the hips and knees extended at the top isn't a complete burpee, so extra burpees are required. An athlete who runs past the penalty loop has broken the rules: record the headband number, document it, and report it to the Head Referee.

rules.title: Scope
rules.excerpt: The following rules of competition ("Rules") are set forth and governed by Spartan and apply to all Spartan events and competitions globally. These Rules are binding on all competitors participating in any Spartan event.

rules.title: Purpose
rules.excerpt: These Rules explain how a race should be officiated and seek to: ensure all Spartan events are conducted in a fair and consistent manner, with sportsmanship and integrity; provide clear guidelines for globally standardized competition; and protect the health, safety and well-being of competitors.

rules.title: Categories
rules.excerpt: The various types of competitor levels are defined as either: Competitive, which includes Elite and Age Group, and Open, which is open to everyone.

rules.title: Head Official
rules.excerpt: A person designated by Spartan as the chief decision maker on all matters of Rules at any event, and the ultimate authority for enforcing and interpreting these Rules.

rules.title: Official
rules.excerpt: Any representative of Spartan designated to carry out event activities and responsibilities in a position of authority. This includes staff members, referees, and volunteers.

rules.title: Heats and waves
rules.excerpt: Groups of competitors belonging to a category and separated by individual start times and/or pace groups.

rules.title: Referee
rules.excerpt: A Spartan appointed official tasked to ensure that all Rules are adhered to, usually posted at obstacles and in the video review tent, reporting to the Head Official.

rules.title: Race Director
rules.excerpt: The Spartan appointed person responsible for the overall operations and execution of a Spartan event.

rules.title: Competition standard
rules.excerpt: All Competitive category racers are expected to explicitly follow all of these Rules. Open category racers are also encouraged to abide by these Rules, despite the more relaxed atmosphere. The Head Official is ultimately responsible for the execution and upholding of these Rules.

rules.title: Starting in the assigned heat
rules.excerpt: All competitors shall start in and with their assigned starting heat, wave or group. Any competitor who starts in an incorrect heat shall be ineligible for awards including qualification to any championship events.

rules.title: Elite racers in the wrong heat
rules.excerpt: Elite competitors who do not start in the correct heat will be moved to the Open category.

rules.title: Two categories of obstacle
rules.excerpt: Obstacles are separated into 2 categories, Mandatory Obstacles and Pass/Fail Obstacles.

rules.title: Failing a mandatory obstacle
rules.excerpt: The penalty for the failure of Mandatory Obstacles is disqualification from the event. At the race director's discretion a time penalty can be substituted for a disqualification depending on the severity of the infraction.

rules.title: Official video review
rules.excerpt: Prior to race results being considered final, an official video review process should take place. Because of this, an event's final results may not be posted on-site immediately, pending the outcome of this official review.

rules.title: Protest period
rules.excerpt: A competitor protest period for penalties, timing and results, disqualifications, or other penalties issued starts immediately after a competitor crosses the finish line and ends 15 minutes prior to the official award ceremony time for their respective Category.

rules.title: Protests go to the Head Official
rules.excerpt: Any protest regarding penalties, or other issues that affect the outcome of the race, must be brought to the Head Official during the protest period. The Head Official may extend a protest period beyond the award ceremony at their sole discretion.

rules.title: Elite timing: gun time
rules.excerpt: The winner of each Elite Category heat is determined by "gun time" or whoever crosses the finish line first, regardless of when they crossed the starting line, with the addition of any time penalties assessed by the Head Official.

rules.title: Chip time
rules.excerpt: The winner of Age Group and Open Category heats, along with Elite category Stadion race heats, will be determined by "Chip Time", the accumulated time from crossing the start line to crossing the finish line, with the addition of any time penalties assessed by the Head Official.

rules.title: Doubles: rules of participation
rules.excerpt: Open category doubles are also encouraged to abide by these Rules in the spirit of sportsmanship and personal accountability. All Open category competitors are expected to use Spartan honor in completing burpee penalties, as they apply to other Open category races.

rules.title: Striking bells
rules.excerpt: Competitors may only strike bells using their arms and hands, or any other part of their body above their chest. Using feet, legs, or knees to kick the bell is an obstacle failure: the competitor may not retry and must complete the mandatory penalty.

rules.title: Interference from another competitor
rules.excerpt: In the case of obstacle failure caused by significant physical interference from another competitor, the affected competitor may restart the obstacle with no additional penalty after receiving permission from an Official.

rules.title: Male and female completion options
rules.excerpt: Obstacles may have different male and female completion options. Where present, competitors are required to complete the option based on their registered gender category. Female competitors may choose to forgo using a female specific kicker or step.

rules.title: 6, 7, 8 and 9 foot walls
rules.excerpt: Climb up and over the wall without using the support bracing, the sides of the wall, flag poles, or straps. Failure: inability to climb over and descend; using the support structure, sides or straps; male competitors using the red step designated for female use only.

rules.title: Rope Climb
rules.excerpt: Climb up the rope and ring the bell. Failure: not ringing the bell; ringing it with the body below the waist; using more than one rope during a single attempt. A competitor may change ropes after returning to the ground and attempt the obstacle multiple times.

rules.title: Ape Hanger
rules.excerpt: Climb the rope or rope ladder, transfer to the bars, traverse using only the hands, and ring the bell. A competitor is committed and considered to have made an attempt once they touch any of the overhead bars, and must then complete the obstacle or the penalty.

rules.title: Bucket Carry
rules.excerpt: Carry the bucket along the marked course with the same amount of material inside and the lid in place. There is no burpee option for this obstacle. It must be completed. A bucket returned with material missing means redoing the entire marked course with a correctly filled bucket.

rules.title: General conduct
rules.excerpt: Competitors must act in compliance with these Rules; treat fellow competitors, staff, volunteers, spectators and the public with fairness, respect and courtesy; and refrain from abusive, threatening, or insulting language or conduct.

rules.title: Penalties for general conduct
rules.excerpt: Violations of General Conduct may result in a penalty depending on the severity of the violation, as determined at the sole discretion of the Head Official.

rules.title: Race conduct
rules.excerpt: Competitors must cover the official course in its entirety; not intentionally impede another competitor; not accept physical assistance or pacing from anyone other than a Spartan official; and plainly display their race number on their headband at all times.

rules.title: Pacing
rules.excerpt: The pacing of competitors by any person is strictly prohibited: running with or near a competitor, in between obstacles, with the intent of assisting them by giving instruction, coaching, or to set a pace.

rules.title: Penalties in video review
rules.excerpt: During the official video review process Race Officials reserve the right to assess penalties including, but not limited to, a time penalty of 10 minutes or disqualification for obstacle failures and/or infractions.

rules.title: Where review penalties are shown
rules.excerpt: Penalties given during this review are made available inside the Results Tent throughout the official video review process.

rules.title: Truss
rules.excerpt: The main supporting structure of an obstacle typically seen as metal tubed diagonal, vertical, and horizontal load bearing beams and supports.

rules.title: Acts warranting suspension
rules.excerpt: Grounds for suspension include flagrant or willful violation of the Rules, gross or continued unsportsmanlike conduct, and physical violence directed toward a race official, competitor, volunteer, spectator, or another person.

rules.title: Footage from competitors and spectators
rules.excerpt: Race Officials are not obligated to review or consider any video or still image captured by competitors, spectators or persons not acting in an official capacity during the video review process.

rules.title: Hercules Hoist
rules.excerpt: Lower the weight so that it is under control and not in a state of freefall when it touches the ground. Fail: dropping the weight to the ground in an uncontrolled manner for any reason.

rules.title: Helix
rules.excerpt: Using only the bars in a single lane, laterally navigate the obstacle without touching the top, and ring the bell. Fail: touching the ground, touching the top, or using bars from another lane. Committed once four points of contact are made.

rules.title: Monkey Bars
rules.excerpt: Traverse using only the hands and arms and ring the bell. Fail: feet touching the ground to create an advantage; using vertical truss as a ladder; feet or legs touching the bars; failure to ring the bell. Horizontal truss may be used to start or transfer.

rules.title: Multi-Rig
rules.excerpt: Traverse using only the attachments, without grabbing the ropes, sling, chains or other elements that affix them, within one lane, and ring the bell. An attempt once both feet have left the starting step.

rules.title: Olympus
rules.excerpt: Laterally navigate using only hands upon and within the holds and holes in a single lane, and ring the bell. Fail: touching the ground, touching the top, or touching any holds or holes with feet. Feet and knees may rest against the wall.

rules.title: Z Wall
rules.excerpt: Laterally traverse using only the hand and foot blocks and upright supports in a single lane, and ring the bell. Fail: touching the ground, the top of the wall, any brace structures, or the top or bottom of any cutouts. Committed at four points of contact.

rules.title: Swim / water crossing
rules.excerpt: Pass through the water from one end to the other while staying within the marked course at all times. No diving. Fail: leaving the boundaries or skirting the obstacle, or diving.

disputes.title: When the protest period ends
disputes.detail: Rules 3.19.1 and 3.19.2: the protest period ends 15 minutes before the official award ceremony for the category (3.19.3: the Head Official may extend it). SOP 4.2: the Head Referee confirms until when protests are allowed, giving "half an hour prior to Award Ceremony" as the example; SOP 4.2.3: referee-error corrections for podium athletes before awards, all others within two hours after final awards. Not covered in the online programme.

disputes.title: When commitment starts on single-attempt obstacles (in general)
disputes.detail: Rules 2.1.7: commitment is as defined in each obstacle's own rules, which differ (for example 4.2.7 Monkey Bars and 4.2.8 Multi-Rig: both feet leave the starting step; 4.2.2 Ape Hanger: touching any overhead bar; 4.2.13 Spear Throw: release in a forward motion). Online programme 4.4: commitment begins once attempt motion starts, for single-attempt obstacles generally.

disputes.title: Who decides burpee penalties when there is no video
disputes.detail: Rules 3.18.2: Race Officials assess penalties during the official video review. SOP 6.iii: where video is available, burpee quantity and quality are decided in video review; where it is not, the Referee on site decides, documents it in writing and submits it to the Head Referee. Online programme 6.3: penalty decisions are made by the video review team (5.4: video review determines missed burpees).

disputes.title: Brief contact that gives no advantage
disputes.detail: Rules 4.2.6 (Helix), 4.2.10 (Olympus) and 4.2.17 (Z Wall): touching the top of the obstacle is a failure mode, with no advantage test; the advantage test appears only in some failure modes, such as feet touching the ground at the Monkey Bars (4.2.7). Online programme 2.4: focus on rule intent, not minor accidental contact; scenario 9.3: an athlete briefly touches the top with no advantage, and referees should consider whether advantage was created and whether a penalty is appropriate.
